item.title: 10 Deadly Sins of a Junior Product Manager
item.description:
This article was originally published on habr.com.

These «deadly sins» can serve as a self-assessment checklist for both junior and more experienced managers.

So, here are the mistakes — and how to fix them.

1. Believing in Multitasking

Every product manager faces enormous flows of information — countless initiatives and product development ideas that no single person can possibly process within the time available. Stakeholders push their agendas, users complain, the calendar is packed with meetings, and the Product Backlog grows by the day.

item.title: Thinking Through Writing
item.description:
I came across a fascinating interview with Andrei Styskin (Director at Amazon, former CEO of the search division at Yandex), in which he talks about some interesting aspects of Amazon’s internal culture — in particular, its «document-centric» approach to meetings and decision-making.

  1. Every work meeting is a collaborative exercise where participants work through a pre-prepared document on a specific problem. Part of the time (10 to 20 minutes) is spent reading the document individually; the rest is spent discussing and commenting on it. If open questions remain after the meeting, another meeting is scheduled in the same format. The process continues until requirements are unambiguously defined and agreed upon by all stakeholders.
  2. Requirements for any product or feature are developed using the «Working Backwards» method — by writing two documents: a «Press Release» and an «FAQ.» Long before launch, the product manager writes a press release that articulates a vision of the ideal outcome, giving the entire product team a north star to orient around throughout development.
  3. All decisions are made through document reviews, not through verbal conversations in meetings or over a smoke break — as often happens in many workplaces.

Reflecting on my time at Yandex (a great company, though not quite in the same league globally — for context, Yandex’s market cap in 2024 was around $10 billion, while Amazon’s was $2 trillion), I can say that Yandex’s internal culture also encourages employees to express their thinking in writing: detailed wiki documentation is standard practice; task tracker descriptions are written out thoroughly; discussions happen in comments; and internal blogs — both public and anonymous — are common. The more senior the person, the more persuasively and concisely they tend to work with text.

item.title: On the Certified Scrum Product Owner Certification
item.description:
In his book Empowered: Ordinary People, Extraordinary Products, Marty Cagan recommends that aspiring product managers get CSPO training and certification early in their careers. I want to share what you can actually expect from this training — beyond just another badge to collect (and a fairly pricey one at that).

The training runs two full days. The first day covers the fundamentals of Agile and Scrum through group exercises, with a brief overview of other product development methodologies. For those just entering the profession, this day is genuinely valuable — it builds a deeper, more intentional understanding of Scrum. That knowledge is useful as a foundation for evaluating and comparing the processes at your own company or on your product.

More experienced product managers will find it helpful for formalizing and structuring what they already know. Most of us work directly with development teams, and a fresh perspective can spark new ideas around creativity and engagement within the team.
